summary: Describes a YANG library giving information about YANG modules, datastores and datastore schemas used by a network management server, with simple caching so clients can avoid re-reading it. It supports the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: A server keeps a list of the rule books it understands. A client reads the list to see what can be managed.

questions: how to list yang modules on a server
what is a yang module set
subtitle: A standard list a network management server publishes of the YANG modules, datastores and schemas it uses.

tldr.problem: A client managing a device needs to know which YANG modules, datastores and datastore schemas the server uses. The earlier YANG library assumed every datastore has exactly the same schema, which does not hold under the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8525 defines the ietf-yang-library module. It lists module sets, the schemas built from them, and the datastores that use each schema, plus a content identifier that changes whenever the information changes.
tldr.outcome: Clients can read the library once, cache it and refetch only when the content identifier changes. RFC 8525 obsoletes RFC 7895 and has since been updated by RFC 10035.

today: RFC 8525 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7895, and it has been updated by RFC 10035.

sections.title: Why a YANG Library Is Needed
sections.content:
Network management servers describe their data with YANG modules, and clients need a standard way to learn which modules, datastores and datastore schemas a given server uses. RFC 8525 defines the YANG module ietf-yang-library to expose exactly that.

The previous version, from RFC 7895, is not compatible with the NMDA because it assumes all datastores have exactly the same schema. Under the NMDA a dynamic configuration datastore can have its own schema, and the operational state datastore may support non-configurable modules in addition to those of conventional configuration datastores.

The library can be different on every server and can change at runtime or across a reboot. If a server offers several management protocols, each one may have its own conceptual instance of the library.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a toy box with a list on the lid saying which games are inside. This RFC says how every toy box should write that list, so anyone can read it.

sections.title: What a Client Needs to Know
sections.content:
For each module the library must tell a client its name, its revision (taken from the most recent revision statement), the name and revision of each submodule, each supported feature, and each module that applies deviations to it. For each datastore it must give the datastore's identity and the schema it implements.

The design was picked against six criteria. Among them: the data must be efficient for a client to consume and cacheable; a dynamic configuration datastore must be able to implement a module or feature that the conventional datastores do not; a module may be left out of <operational> even if other datastores implement it; and a given module can only be implemented in one revision across all datastores. It must also work with schema mount.
sections.plainLanguage: Before writing the list, the authors asked what a reader would want to know: the name of each game, which version it is, and which optional parts are switched on.

sections.title: Module Sets, Schemas and Datastores
sections.content:
All data nodes in ietf-yang-library are config false, so they are only accessible in the operational state datastore. Everything sits under one /yang-library container with four kinds of child.

  • module-set: named collections of modules. Each module entry carries its submodules, features and deviations. An import-only-module entry lists modules used only for imports.
  • schema: each entry refers to one or more module sets, and the schema is the union of all modules in them. All conventional configuration datastores use the same schema entry.
  • datastore: one entry per datastore the server supports, pointing at its schema.
  • content-id: a single identifier for the current contents.

Which module set a module is listed in is at the server's discretion, and this revision attaches no meaning to it. A common case is that the operational state datastore schema is a superset of the schema used by conventional configuration datastores.
sections.plainLanguage: Groups of games go in labelled boxes. A shelf is made of one or more boxes, and each room says which shelf it uses.

sections.title: Caching with the Content Identifier
sections.content:
The content-id leaf is an implementation-specific identifier of the current library contents. Its value MUST change whenever the information in the library changes. There is no requirement that the same information always produce the same value.

This lets a client fetch all schema information once, cache it, and refetch only if the value has changed. When it changes, the server also sends a yang-library-update notification.

For a NETCONF server that implements the NETCONF extensions for the NMDA (RFC 8526), a change of the content identifier results in a new value for the :yang-library:1.1 capability. If that server also supports NETCONF notifications and the netconf-capability-change notification, that notification is generated whenever the identifier changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The list has a version stamp. If the stamp is the same as last time, you do not need to read the whole list again.

sections.title: Compatibility with the Old Library
sections.content:
The old definitions from RFC 7895 are kept for backwards compatibility but marked as deprecated, including the /modules-state tree. An NMDA-supporting server SHOULD still populate /modules-state in a backwards-compatible manner. Legacy clients ignore the new /yang-library tree, and NMDA-aware clients ignore /modules-state.

The recommended way to fill /modules-state is to report the modules with config true data nodes that are configurable via conventional configuration datastores, and the modules with config false data nodes that a NETCONF <get> operation or equivalent returns.

Appendix A lists the changes: the title became "YANG Library", a new top-level container holds module sets, schemas and datastores, and the yang-library-update notification replaces the deprecated yang-library-change notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The old list stays on the wall so old visitors can still read it, while a new, better list hangs next to it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, with SSH and TLS as the mandatory-to-implement secure transports. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict which users read which parts.

The /yang-library subtree may help an attacker identify server capabilities and implementations with known bugs, since the set of modules can reveal the kind of device and its manufacturer. Vulnerabilities may be specific to particular modules, revisions, features or deviations, so the module list could help an attacker aim a denial-of-service attack. Read access to these nodes should therefore be controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of everything in the toy box also tells a burglar what is worth taking, so only trusted people should be allowed to read it.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
RFC 7895 had registered one URI in the IETF XML Registry. RFC 8525 takes over that registration and changes the Registrant Contact to the IESG.

It also registers the module in the YANG Module Names registry with the name ietf-yang-library, the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-library and the prefix yanglib.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag for this list is written in the official register so nobody else uses the same name.
